title: Hide Artifacts: Resource Forking
summary: Resource Forking hides payloads in the resource fork, a secondary stream that classic Mac file systems attached to a file beside its normal data. The fork existed for structured items such as icons, dialogs, menus and code, and on modern macOS it appears as an extended attribute that ordinary file views rarely show. An adversary can park an encoded or encrypted payload there, then use a small loader to read the fork and execute its content at a chosen offset. Because the visible file body and its hash stay unchanged, integrity checks that examine only file content pass. Defenders surface the fork with attribute listing tools and treat unexpectedly large attributes on downloaded files as suspicious.

beginner.definition: On macOS, a file can carry more than its normal contents. A resource fork is a second storage area attached to the same file. It was designed to hold things like icons, menus and small code blocks. An attacker can hide a small program there, in a place where normal file viewers do not look.
beginner.whyItMatters: The file itself looks unchanged, so its fingerprint still matches. Tools that compare file hashes see nothing wrong. The hidden part appears only when you ask for extended attributes. This makes a resource fork a quiet place to store a second stage of an attack. Checking the file body alone is not enough on macOS.
howItWorks: A file on macOS can have a main data part and an extra resource part.
The resource part stores structured items such as icons, dialog boxes and small code blocks.
Attackers write an encoded or encrypted payload into the resource part of a normal file.
The visible contents and the file hash stay the same, so simple checks pass.
A small loader reads the hidden part and moves the payload to a runnable location.
Only tools that list extended attributes show that something extra is attached.
beginner.example: Imagine a hardback book on a library shelf. The cover, the title and the number of pages all look normal, and the catalogue entry matches. Someone has cut a hollow space inside the back cover and hidden a small key there. A librarian who checks the title and the page count finds nothing wrong. Only a reader who opens the back cover and feels inside finds the key. A resource fork is that hollow space in the back cover.
takeaways: On macOS, a file can hold hidden data beside its visible contents.
A hash check that reads only file content can miss an attached resource.
List extended attributes on downloaded files before you trust them.

objectives: Explain what a resource fork is and what it was originally designed to store.
Describe how a payload is stored in a fork and later executed.
Identify the commands that display resource fork and attribute data.
Explain why content only integrity checks can miss this hidden payload.
Describe how resource forks relate to the modern application bundle structure.
